preamble: In fast or casual speech a coda /t/ often takes on the bilabial place of a following /p/, /b/ or /m/, giving [p] (regressive place assimilation). The process is asymmetric across languages: coronals assimilate to labials and velars, but labials and velars rarely assimilate to coronals. Articulatory studies show that it is often gradient and can leave a residual alveolar gesture, but perception experiments also find complete changes (sit politely heard as sip politely). Korean has the same optional process at the coda–onset boundary. Standard Korean pronunciation norms explicitly exclude it from standard pronunciation while noting that it occurs in rapid speech.

examples.note: Gaskell and Snoeren (2008) use this example of how place assimilation can make sit sound like sip; their production data show that complete assimilations occur in casual speech.

The coda /t/ (neutralized from ㅊ) assimilates to the following bilabial /p/. Standard Pronunciation Article 21 rejects this form as non-standard but notes that it occurs in rapid speech (also 문법 [문뻡], *[뭄뻡] 'grammar' for n > m).

sources: Gaskell, M. G., & Snoeren, N. D. (2008). The impact of strong assimilation on the perception of connected speech. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance 34(6), 1632–1647. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0011977
